What we know and judge at that point is not absolute nonexistence itself. It is the concept “absolute nonexistence,” which applies to itself as an idea and is present to the mind. We are saying that if this concept pointed to something outside the mind, as a picture points to the thing it represents, then no judgment about the concept could pass over to that outside thing. But it does not point to an outside thing now; it is only an idea. If it did point to such a thing, it would no longer name absolute nonexistence. This is a subtle point. — ن ره
To say that absolute nonexistence cannot be judged means that the concept cannot be used to make a claim about something outside the mind. It has no real-world form for the claim to apply to. — ن ره

The word “some” matters because not every concept fails to apply to itself as a real thing. The concepts “thing,” “universal,” and “essence,” for example, can also apply to themselves in that sense. All concepts apply to themselves in the first, basic sense—as ideas. — س ره
This expands the brief point made earlier. The author could have left it out there. — س ره

Here is how a circular dependence leads to an endless chain. Suppose A depends on B and B depends on A. Then A depends on itself. But what something depends on must be distinct from the dependent thing. So, on this supposition, A and “A itself” must be different. Yet A itself is nothing other than A. We can repeat the argument, replacing A with “A itself,” then with “the self of A itself,” and so on. This produces an endless chain on both sides of the original circle. Al-Sayyid al-Sharif presents the argument this way in his notes on al-Mataliʿ; the details can be found there.

I can give a shorter and firmer explanation. On the assumption of circular dependence, A depends on B, B on A, then A on B again, then B on A, without end. None of these steps establishes that A or B actually exists. They are like a chain of conditions: “If B exists, A exists; if A exists, B exists; if B exists, A exists...” We never reach the point where we can say, “But B exists, therefore A exists,” or the reverse. Nothing establishes the first condition, so the chain cannot stop. — س ره

An accidental conditional can connect true claims: “If a human being speaks, a donkey brays.” Both may happen, but one does not require the other. The cases at issue here are false claims, such as “If a human brays, a horse speaks,” “If two identical things cannot be together, neither can a vacuum,” or “If Zayd does not exist, the phoenix does not exist.” We cannot treat such pairings as true just because both claims are false; at most, they can be supposed together. — س ره

A universal “if … then” statement covers every possible way the first claim may be assumed. So “whenever two is a number, this follows” includes the case where two is assumed to be odd, as in the example. — س ره
The author first denies that existence is added as something separate, then denies that it is attached to the essence as a feature. — س ره
Rather, conceiving something is an act of relation, as the Imam al-Razi holds. — س ره

Not so. Those thinkers too sought to show only that existence and essence differ in our understanding, as we saw earlier. Al-Tusi says as much in Tajrid: existence is added in our mental representations. There may be exceptions among some followers of Aristotle who hold that existence joins essence outside the mind, and among the Muʿtazilites. — س ره

The note clarifies the alternatives. Existence and essence cannot be identical in meaning yet distinct in reality, since one essence has only one existence. If they are called “the same” only in meaning, this does not rule out their being distinct in reality. If they are the same in reality as well, they must be identical in meaning, one must be part of the other, or one must be added to the other. — س ره

This is how the argument appears in Sharh al-Maqasid, but there is a difficulty. The collection of all these added existences has no property beyond the properties of its individual members; nor does it have a separate existence of its own, as we shall explain when we discuss endless chains. Each added existence would have to rest on another existence already present, which would itself be added to the essence. The same would be true without end. We would never reach an existence identical with the essence. — س ره

This critic rejects the claim that an essence must already exist before existence can belong to it. He says that essence may come before existence in what it is, just as it comes before unity, individuality, possibility, and other features that belong to thinghood itself. — س ره

“Essences” here means the things the mind distinguishes from existence. In thought, they are ideas attached to other existences; in ordinary speech, they are themselves called existences. Or the author may mean that they are existences in reality, not merely in thought. Either way, the point is that essence and existence are one outside the mind; otherwise, the view would be al-Ash‘ari’s. — س ره

The things we understand in our minds are reflections of existences first brought into being directly. The word “forms” most likely refers to the general forms that higher realities reflect into the reasoning mind. Another possibility is that their light appears to us and we see those forms directly or become united with them. On this reading, “by reflection from higher realities” concerns nearness and distance from God; “the light of existence appearing within us” concerns how ready or unready we are to receive it. Consider the sun. One person grasps only the ordinary idea of a bright heavenly body; another knows its full nature through the causes on which it depends. The same distinction applies elsewhere. — س ره

This knowledge does not come merely by drawing an idea from things, as people commonly suppose. A Persian verse says: “Free yourself from matter to see what is free of matter. To see anything, this is the condition.” The Qur'an says, “In God's Messenger you have a good example,” and, “Follow their guidance.” It is also reported from the imams: “Our affair is difficult, exceedingly difficult; none can bear it except a messenger sent by God or an angel brought near to Him.” This is what is meant by intercession at the beginning and the end of the journey.

Following their example fills the heart with light and purifies one's inner life until the person reaches the intended goal: knowing things as they truly are through direct experience. While this work prepares the seeker, it is called the path; when it achieves its aim, it is called the reality, and people reach it to differing degrees. I have explained as much as space allows of the subtle meaning suggested here, but few fully attain it. Do not suppose that this contradicts the earlier statement that existence is added to the essences of possible things. — ن ره

Al-Ash‘ari means “existent” in the sense of what is actually real, but for him this reality is the essence itself after a maker brings it into being. He denies that existence has a separate instance, in the mind or outside it, that makes “existent” apply to an essence. The author also grounds the claim that something exists in a kind of union, but he means that the concept “human being,” for example, is united with a particular reality of existence. — س ره

This note challenges the view that existences differ completely in reality. If they do, how can one shared idea be drawn from them? If it can, then the earlier proof that there is only one Necessary Being would fail. — س ره

Calling “existent” an idea formed only when we think about other things seems to conflict with the claim that what it names is a reality in its own right. An idea of this second kind is usually understood not to point directly to a thing existing outside the mind. How, then, are we to understand the claim here? It is no answer simply to give the word “secondary” a new meaning unlike the one these thinkers ordinarily use. — ن ره
The note objects that the concepts divided into primary and secondary are general ideas, not real existences. — ن ره

The soul is existence without an essence beyond it because every description we imagine for it—such as “the first perfection of a body,” “the ruler of the body,” or “a substance separate in itself but not in its actions”—is different from the soul itself. None of these ideas is what we mean by “I” or “my self.” The soul is not beyond substance because it is less than substance, but because it is a reality of existence. The note also says the soul has no fixed limit to its growth; it can always go beyond what it has reached. Scripture says that human beings were created weak and are deeply unjust and ignorant. Existence with no limit has no essence beyond itself. Concepts such as God’s knowledge, will, and power do not describe a limited existence, so they are not essences. An essence is an idea that describes existence with a limit. The same applies to the intellects. — س ره
Here “pure existence” means existence not joined to anything else. “Necessity” means standing on one’s own, as the Shaykh holds of the soul. — ن ره

To claim that only qualities can be stronger or weaker is to make an assertion without proof. Existence itself differs by degrees; other things, such as qualities, are called stronger or weaker because of their relation to existence. The reality of existence ranges from fullness to lack, from independence to need. — ن ره

The Shaykh calls existence one and simple because he believes that a shared idea can be part of what a thing is, while still applying by degrees. If it is part of what things are, then the unity of the idea in the mind reflects unity in reality. The philosophers in Aristotle’s school reject this, since they say that only an added feature can apply by degrees. They therefore think that the same idea in the mind does not prove that the realities themselves are one. The Shaykh also calls existence a “kind” because, if something can apply by degrees and still be the nature of the things it applies to, then existence itself can be that one nature. — س ره

The point is that the general idea of existence is not part of the essences of particular things. It is a mental idea, but in a way it stands for those things as their nature does: it applies to them from the outside without adding another feature to them. If this is so, the one idea reflects a shared reality. Particular existences have no parts, either in the world or in thought, so what they share is also what makes them different. — س ره

The note explains why a particular thing needs the general idea: if that idea were absent, the particular would also be absent. The reverse does not always follow. If a cause is absent, its effect is absent; but if a condition is present, the thing that needs it does not have to be present. The author’s wording sets out two related points, rather than repeating one point twice. — س ره

If they mean the general idea of existence, their view makes the Necessary Being nonexistent. If they mean an all-pervading existence present in every thing, it makes every existent—including filth—the Necessary Being. The first follows if “absolute existence” means a concept; the second follows if it means something present in all instances. I would add: if they mean the reality of existence without any limit, even the limit of being called “absolute,” there is no problem—provided they mean the reality that encompasses all things. — س ره

The absence of everything is not impossible in itself. It is impossible only because it would also remove one thing that cannot be absent in itself—the Necessary Being. The same is true of denying all causality: that would remove a particular kind of causality that cannot be absent. — ه ره

Calling existence in general a secondary idea seems to conflict with saying that it has one real instance, God, or many real instances. The same issue arises when the author says that a general concept has real instances. But “secondary idea” here means only that existence in general, as a general idea, has no reality outside the mind. That is clear enough, though this is not unique to secondary ideas: no general idea, even a basic one, exists outside the mind in its general form. The note says this will be explained later. — س ره
The same observation appears in Sharh al-Maqasid by al-Taftazani. — س ره
This means the general, self-evident idea of existence. — س ره

“Shares” here means manifestations of existence. A share in a concept differs from the concept only through a relation or condition, which is itself only an idea. Outside the mind, a manifestation is existence appearing in a particular essence that is absorbed in it. The philosophers call this an “illuminating relation.” In one respect, a name is the thing named; in another, it is different—just as the image of a thing in the mind is that thing in one way, but not in every way. — س ره

“Shared” may mean that existence is universal because it encompasses all things. One could also say it is particular, if “particular” means that it is distinct in itself—not that it is a general kind surrounded by features that make it individual. — س ره

Perhaps the author says existence applies by degrees because its real instances have different levels. The difference among them is then attributed to the general idea of existence. Otherwise, we would have to say that ideas themselves apply by degrees. The note says the author seems to allow this in some later discussions. — ط
These views bring together the main points made from the beginning of this book, as an alert reader will see. — س ره

If existence itself differs by degrees, then it has many levels. These levels differ in relation to one another: one may lack something that another has, and one may be less complete than the other. Yet they all share the same basic reality. We can divide existence into mental and external, potential and actual, many and one, then say that existence itself is external, actual, and one. This is what the author means when he says that existence in itself is simply real and actual. — ط
This note clarifies the words “even though.” — س ره

The phrase “existence is the things themselves” may mean that existence is what is most real in each thing. Given the words that follow, it may also point to a higher vision in which the forms of things fade from view and only the light of God remains. In this vision, the traveler sees the All-Hearing and All-Seeing rather than an animal; the Subtle and All-Aware rather than a spirit; the Holy and Pure rather than an angel; the Ever-Living and Exalted rather than the heavens; and the Greatest Name rather than Adam. The note quotes the saying, “My knowledge of the luminous is knowledge of God,” and connects this to the Qur'anic words “When God’s help and victory come,” and to the saying, “The height of sincerity is to deny attributes of Him.” In this vision the cycles of outward appearances end and the divine names come into view; it goes beyond even seeing the Named, where the names themselves fall away. The note compares the passage to a Persian line in al-Tusi’s Aghaz va Anjam: “Praise belongs to God: all beings begin from Him and all return to Him—indeed, all are He Himself.” It presents this as another possible way to understand the author’s words. — س ره

Essences and fixed realities are forms of God’s names, attributes, and their effects. In the level of divine oneness, they share one existence with the names and attributes, since they are realized through the One named, though their meanings differ. — س ره

The names and attributes follow from existence in meaning, but in reality they are one with it. Later, the author will show that life, knowledge, will, power, and other perfections follow existence wherever it appears and are joined to it. — س ره
This points to God’s all-sustaining presence, and to His being first in reality while all else comes after Him. — ن ره

These words are reported from Ali, whose speech is described as God’s speech: “With everything, but not by being beside it; different from everything, but not by being apart from it.” In another place: “Within things, but not by mixing; beyond things, but not by separation.” Elsewhere: “He is not inside things by entering them, nor outside them by leaving them.” — س ره

“Within things without mixing, beyond them without separation” means that God is not inside things as one thing is inside another, nor outside them as one thing leaves another. The difference is in His quality, not in being cut off from them. — ن ره

The note names six levels of divine self-disclosure: oneness, divine unity, the world of power, the world of spirits, the visible world, and the all-comprehensive human realm. It says that the six days during which God’s light is hidden correspond to these levels, as in the Qur'anic account of the creation of the heavens and the earth in six days. — س ره

Al-Saduq says in The Beliefs that souls and spirits remain after death; some are blessed and some punished, until they return to their bodies at the resurrection. The commentator says this does not conflict with God ending things at the first trumpet by hiding them when the light of oneness shines and they fade from view. This is a deep divine mystery, not what the words may seem to mean at first. — ن ره

This means that essences appear in detail in the outside world, while in God’s all-encompassing knowledge they were already present without names or distinctions. The note quotes the mystic poet Jami: “The world’s essences, beyond how and why, were hidden from both knowledge and sight. No mark of their being was written on the tablet of knowledge; they had not yet drawn strength from the gift of existence.” — س ره
This follows the author’s view that the soul creates forms, drawing them from hidden and unseen states into visible levels. — س ره

The author’s qualification “when thinking of them as images” answers a possible objection. Someone might say that mental images can cause things: without an imagined building or fire, no building or fire would be made outside the mind. Or that they can be affected, since they have essences that can receive forms. Or that they can be stable, since imagined forms—and even more so intellectual ones—are more stable than material things. The answer is that the author means images considered as tools for viewing external things. From this point of view, they are appearances of those things. He is also explaining their special status: they are not active like separate intellects or receptive like material forms. — س ره

Mental existence is defined by contrast with external existence: an external thing has its characteristic effects, while a mental thing does not. But mental things have effects of their own: they remove ignorance, have a distinct form in the mind, and can produce reactions such as blushing from shame or turning pale from fear. In these respects, they are real in the mind. Every mental thing is measured against something outside the mind; whatever has no counterpart outside the mind has no mental form either. And things whose very nature is to be external and to produce external effects—such as existence in its pure external sense and the Necessary Being—cannot be present in the mind in that way. — ط

Anything present to another thing must first exist in itself, and its presence removes one kind of nonexistence from that other thing. This is what we mean by a feature or quality: it is present to something after the lack of it has been removed. So everything present to another is a feature of it in this broad sense, though it belongs to the other only at the level where it removes that lack. An effect is present to its cause in this way: it removes a lack in the cause at the level where the cause’s action is complete. The note says this gives a clue to how God’s active attributes arise, a matter to be explained later. — ط
The soul is not always weak in itself. Its weakness here comes from its role as a mirror for the images of particular things. — س ره

The author says “estimation,” not “imagination,” because the estimating faculty directs the brain’s powers and grasps particular meanings such as love, fear, wishes, and hopes. Each of these has its own image. For example, intense fear in a dark graveyard or wilderness may make the imagination form a frightening shape, perhaps a demon or monster. Intense love and longing may make a lover imagine that the beloved is present. Through wishes, hopes, fears, and desires, people form images of what they want, dread, or love. Most people attend either to the things themselves when they are present or to the images their minds create when they are absent. Only the most devoted attend to God, the Creator of all these forms. The philosophers say that simple intellects create the detailed forms of intellect. — س ره
“Knower” may mean someone who knows realities in detail, someone able to act in existence, or someone with both abilities. Here it means the second or third kind. — س ره

“Outside the place of imagination” means outside the knower’s own imagination. This distinguishes true creation from magic or sleight of hand, which may show images outside the magician’s imagination but only by influencing the imaginations of the audience. — ه ره

The five realms are the divine realm, the realm of power, the realm of spirits, the visible human world, and the all-encompassing human realm. The human realm itself can contain and preserve the ordered, unseen realms above the world of meanings and fixed realities. — س ره
The word “and” begins a new sentence here. It does not describe a state or join this point to the previous one, which would make the passage contradict itself. — س ره

The passage through “the forms preserve one another” describes the knower’s awareness of all the realms. The following passage describes the fact that a knower must always be present to at least one realm. Every thing that exists outside the mind passes through all the levels of knowledge before appearing. One form can preserve the others because a form in a higher realm is the cause, spirit, and meaning of the forms below it. A lower form reveals its higher cause, since an effect points back to its cause and an image represents its meaning. — س ره

This means that no one is entirely inattentive—not ordinary people and not the special few. Ordinary people also witness a display of reality, though they may not know what is appearing through it. — س ره

A person creates and preserves things through resolve, but even when the person creates an act, God is the true Creator. “There is no power or strength except through God, the Most High and Mighty.” — س ره

The note says the reply as given is not quite right. If the mental form is simply the reality of the known thing, with no difference between the two, then there is no distinction between a thing and its mental counterpart; this seems to deny mental existence. The philosophers mean that an essence remains the same while its existence differs, which would allow a counterpart and bring back the original problem. The reply’s phrase “shadow-like appearance” may mean only that the mind is related to the reality known. But if it means a separate existence for the form, then the same question arises about the essence shared by different kinds of existence. The better answer is that each thing has a counterpart suited to its own nature. For a nonexistent thing, the counterpart is precisely the lack of any external reality. Its mental form is also an idea of absence, not a different object. The mistake is to assume that a counterpart must always be something that exists.
Knowledge of nonexistent things was explained earlier by distinguishing a thing’s basic meaning from the fact that it is absent. Absolute nonexistence is absent in its very nature. — س ره
The supposition itself is real as a thought, but “flies” is stated as an actual feature. So the subject must have some actual existence. — س ره

A universal statement concerns whatever falls under a general title in reality, whether its examples exist outside the mind, are only possible, or do not exist at all. If the statement is to apply to those real or possible examples, it cannot be limited to actual external things. Since the subject understood in this way is not present outside the mind, it must be present within it. — س ره

The shared idea exists in the mind, but we do not have to consider it as existing there. Its commonness comes from the mind’s way of considering it. In many places, the author holds that commonness comes from existence itself—specifically, a dependent mental existence—rather than from essence by itself. This may be what he means when he says that the point will be explained later. — س ره

“Applies to them” does not mean that the mental universal is literally predicated of external individuals as one and the same thing. The proof concerns an idea in the mind. The essence considered only as a kind, apart from its material features, can be said to be the same as the individuals; but mental existence and universality cannot be separated from the essence in the mind. Here, “same” means that the idea shares the individuals’ basic nature. The universal term that can truly be applied to each person is the nature “human being,” considered without a condition. — س ره

The word 'natural' is unnecessary here and would be better omitted, as the author’s later words make clear. A thing’s nature, considered by itself—not even as the subject of a general idea—exists outside the mind. The error is to confuse that nature with the general idea of it in our minds. — س ره
This is true: the idea that applies to many is the natural kind, which is indistinct from its individual examples in its basic meaning. The argument still works, as the author says. — س ره

This argument assumes that anything that exists for something else must exist in the same place where that relation applies. Some philosophers instead say that a relation’s being true of a thing requires only that the thing it describes exist, not that the relation itself exist in that same place. The author may mean that ideas drawn from things, though they do not exist outside the mind, still have a real standing. For example, being Zayd’s father or owning a horse is not an external object; these are relations we understand in the mind. The note says this point, despite its qualifications, belongs to the first method. — س ره

Ali is reported to have said, “I tore down the gate of Khaybar through God’s power, not through bodily strength.” A Persian poem makes the same point: “The power and action of God rose through him; he uprooted Khaybar’s gate by a force beyond his own. And what is Khaybar? Even the fortress of heaven would have been weak before that hand.” — س ره

Knowledge, like life, will, and other perfections, accompanies existence wherever it is found. Indeed, these perfections are one with existence itself. Natural beings have existence, though it is incomplete and mixed with potential and lack. They also have a weak kind of knowledge and life. The Qur'an says, “There is nothing that does not praise Him, though you do not understand their praise.” This awareness is basic knowledge, not the power to feel through touch. Otherwise, plants would be animals, since an animal can sense and move by choice. A thing in nature does not reach sensation until its powers of movement have developed, as the stages of life require. There is also another answer: natural things act under the direction of higher powers that know the ends toward which they are directed. A shot arrow moves toward a goal, but the archer knows the goal, not the arrow. In the same way, natural things may be directed toward ends that are known by the powers directing them. — س ره

This meaning differs from the previous one. The previous one was “what exists as existing,” meaning existence itself. This one is an essence that actually exists. It differs from the last meaning because it includes actual existence and the condition “not in a subject,” while the last meaning includes neither. — س ره

The concept of something existing in a subject—which is what an accident is—cannot be a broad category for the nine kinds of accidents. That would conflict with the philosophers’ view that these nine are the highest categories. al-Muhaqqiq al-Damad does say that substance and accident are two broad categories. But the better view is that “accident” describes how these things exist in relation to something else. An essential feature belongs to a thing without reference to anything outside it. In truth, an accident has a dependent kind of existence: its existence in itself is the same as its existence in the subject it depends on. Even if most philosophers leave relation out of their definitions, they agree that it belongs to the way these things exist. Since being an accident means having a relational existence, and existence is not part of a thing’s basic nature, being an accident is not essential to it. — س ره

This means considering something with a condition, or without one. By “taking the universal where the particular belongs,” the author means treating the general idea as if it were the particular magnet. — س ره

Earlier in this commentary, the natural universal was explained as a nature that can be considered in several ways: by itself, joined to other conditions, or separated from them. It is even more open-ended than an unrestricted nature, since it can take on many conditions that cannot coexist. This is what the author means when he says it can be joined to incompatible conditions. Other writers use “natural universal” for a nature considered without any condition; the author calls this an intellectual universal. al-Taftazani writes in The Refinement of Logic that its subject is natural. Some copies read, “as the essence described as universal is called an intellectual universal.” On that reading, the meaning is clear. — س ره

Many things do not fall under the ten categories, such as particular possible existences, which are not necessary existents, and simple distinguishing features. These are either particular existences, as the author holds, or simple natures that do not belong to any category, as other philosophers hold. Even some qualities, such as a point or unity, do not belong to the nine categories in their view. — س ره

The first problem was answered earlier. The second and third are these: a general idea is universal as an idea, yet it exists in a particular mind, and its subject is one of the things that makes it particular. How, then, can it be both general and particular? Also, in their view, knowledge and the thing known are one. Yet knowledge of blackness belongs to the knower, not to blackness itself. God’s knowledge of things is identical with His being, but the things He knows are not. The commentator then explains the view with a mirror example. Imagine a person standing before a mirror, with his body reflected in it. There are two images: the person’s natural image, which is not in the mirror, and the reflection on the mirror’s surface, which depends on the mirror. The view says that the mind works like a mirror. For each thing we perceive, it posits three forms: the external thing, known indirectly; a mental form, which is present to the mind but does not depend on it; and a form that depends on the mind, which this view calls the external thing. Each form has its own subject. — س ره

This view combines two positions. It says that the form in the mind is like the external thing in its nature and features, while the form that depends on the mind is its shadow because it is a quality. The actual external thing, meanwhile, belongs to another category. Or else it invents a third position by claiming there are two forms: those who say the mental form is a likeness, and those who say it is a shadow, each speak of only one form. No one spoke of two. — س ره

The point is to show the flaw in saying that what exists in the mind, apart from the mind, is general and immaterial. Generality and being free of matter depend on its existence for the mind. This also supports the author’s claim that there must be a causal link: the mind must be one of the causes of what exists in it. — س ره

Just because a thing exists for another in the same way it exists in itself, it does not follow that it must exist inside that other thing. The claim cannot simply be turned around. But here the point is that a mental form cannot exist for the mind in the way that something produced exists for its maker. The mind, especially when it is only potentially able to understand, receives forms passively. So this particular kind of existence for the mind must mean that the form depends on the mind. — س ره

That is, the mental form is not in matter and is not covered by material features. The author says that, if this form did not depend on the mind, it would have to be particular and perceptible, not general and intelligible. The author is showing that the other view leads to a contradiction, as his words “we assumed it was intelligible” make clear. According to that view, the mind frees forms from matter by removing their material features. But that process depends on the forms existing for the mind. If the forms do not depend on the mind, they remain material, whatever names one gives them. — س ره
This is the position he takes on mental forms to answer several objections.
This objection will arise in two forms later, in the section of this book on the intellect and what it knows. — س ره

Someone might say that the reverse must also follow. The answer is that there is no quality in the mind, as we will explain when discussing God’s knowledge and the beings that govern the kinds of things. All these forms exist through the soul’s existence. Their concepts, of course, can be applied to themselves in the basic, definitional sense. — س ره

The phrase “their relation to bodily kinds” can be read as referring either to the intellectual forms themselves or to the forms together with the ideas drawn from them. On the author’s view, and on Plato’s, the objects of intellect are the intellectual realities seen from afar in the creative world.

The author distinguishes the soul’s perception of sensed and imagined forms from its perception of intellectual forms. It brings the first about through its own activity, but reaches the second through an illuminating connection. Why? Individual forms are marked by size, shape, change, and limits. So the author often says that the soul perceives them by making them. He sometimes describes this as union, since these forms are the soul’s own lights and appearances, not separate things. As a saying about the appearance of the First Reality puts it: “All are expressions; You are the meaning, the magnet of hearts.”

General forms, by contrast, are marked chiefly by unity, freedom from matter, and their reach across the subtle details of imagined and natural things. They rise above both worlds and both regions. So the author says that the soul knows them by becoming one with them. This is what he means by an illuminating connection and by direct, present knowledge. Such knowledge can occur through union or through causation. Causation does not fit here, though some writers sometimes say that the simple intellect or soul creates detailed intellects and forms of knowledge. The author has reasons for rejecting this, including his reply to al-Qushji. So union is what remains.

If you ask what he says about general ideas that have no separate intellectual beings as their source, he says they too represent the sources of existing things, but they are labels that do not accurately fit them. Even an inaccurate definition points toward the thing it is meant to define. To see how this can happen, consider how the light of existence reaches even its opposite, nonexistence, including absolute nonexistence, and an essence considered apart from existence. We can understand universal existence—the most obvious and wide-reaching thing—by seeing from afar the light of existence itself, which is brighter and wider than any light or shadow. In the higher world, a quality and the thing it belongs to are one, just as the scent of musk and the musk itself are one; otherwise, potentiality would follow.

Many minds find the idea that knowing a general form means seeing the source of a kind unsettling. The author discusses the reasons elsewhere. Most come down to two. First, people treat a concept as if it were the whole reality and overlook existence itself: its unity includes all its levels and details, so it can both know and be known. Second, they treat the general idea only as a mirror for looking at particular things, instead of turning it around and seeing what the idea itself reveals. — س ره

This does not mean a limited kind of existence, such as the existence of water, fire, or other natural things. It means another, form-like and luminous existence for these natures, unlike their dark material existence, which cannot support knowledge. The author means that the existence of natures in the mind—in the signs within the soul—is like their existence in external things—in the signs of the world. Just as external existence is God’s sacred outpouring and illuminating act, not a substance or quality in itself, so knowledge is an existence that flows from the soul and is lit by it; in itself, it is neither a substance nor a quality. The natures themselves are substances, quantities, and qualities in the basic, definitional sense, not in the ordinary sense. This distinction between the two ways of applying a term matters to the argument that follows. The reply rests on two points: things in the mind are themselves in the basic sense, not in the ordinary sense; and the forms are truly qualities, not merely called qualities as a figure of speech. The reply accepts the familiar philosophical principles; the author has already offered other answers that do not depend on them. — س ره

The author says “in our view,” even though everyone agrees that a nature considered by itself is neither existent nor nonexistent. The reason is that those who treat a nature as a real thing are, in effect, saying that it exists in itself, though they may say it exists only through its relation to its maker, as the author says of existence. They accept the point in words, while the results of their view imply it. As Imam al-Razi says, the claim that a nature is not made follows from the question of what a nature is in itself. — س ره

At first, this seems to conflict with the author’s earlier claim that universality comes from intellectual existence itself. But intellectual existence is so wide that it extends evenly across all its details. In the section on the soul, he says that the generality and individuality of an intellectual form are not two separate things. How, then, can its nature be general? Perhaps he means that generality comes from the nature’s lack of individual features and its great openness, as he suggests here. Its ability to apply to many comes from being seen from afar, with its inner reality not fully grasped. “They forgot God, so He made them forget themselves.” Or perhaps he means that the nature does not resist being general, as something able to receive that feature, though it does not require generality by itself. The discussion of the soul makes this point clearer. — س ره

This is the standard definition of a human being, though it can be challenged. A definition may tell us what truly makes a thing what it is, or it may merely help us tell that thing apart from others. Here we need the first kind. So the definition should include each level it passes through: its material and mineral form, its ability to have dimensions, growth, the senses, the powers that prompt and carry out movement, voluntary movement, and reason both as a capacity and in use. A thing cannot reach a higher kind until it has all the conditions of a lower kind. If “mineral form” is included under “able to have dimensions,” then growth and sensation should be included too. Otherwise the definition does not show all the essential parts. It is not enough simply to distinguish humans; the words “rational” or even “laughing” would do that. A full definition would be: a human being is a substance that can have dimensions, has an elemental and mineral form, grows, senses, moves by choice, and reasons. — س ره
This follows the common view. The author will discuss later whether it is a quality only incidentally. — س ره
Ordinary predication concerns the shared existence of subject and predicate, and existence is incidental to an essence. The second kind of predication is different. — س ره

Predication requires a difference in one way and identity in another. When a definition is said of the thing it defines, the difference is between the general and the detailed meaning. For example, “human being” is “animal that reasons.” The two are the same in nature, but one is the full definition and the other is the thing defined. The phrase “human being is human being” can also have meaning if someone has first suggested that a human being can be separated from itself. The reply says that the human being whose existence you question is exactly the human being whose existence cannot be denied. Similarly, when philosophers say that a human being, considered just as a human being, is only itself, they mean that it is neither existent, nonexistent, nor anything else beyond its own nature. This is not empty repetition: it says that the two meanings are identical, not merely that they share an existence. — س ره

“Essence” here means the actual thing or example. If two concepts are identical, they share an existence; but the reverse does not always follow. Primary predication is about identity of meaning. The existence in question may be actual, mental, or merely assumed. Claims such as “nothing is nothing” or “contradictions are contradictions” use this kind of predication, even though they have no actual existence. — س ره

For example, “a laughing person is a writer” and “a laughing person is not a writer” can both be true in different senses: one may be a writer in actual existence without being one by nature. The concept “laughing person,” which is shared by all people who laugh, is “laughing” by primary predication but not by ordinary predication. — س ره

The author means natures considered without any condition—the natural universals discussed before the two kinds of predication. He does not mean “intellectual universals” in the usual technical sense. This is clear from his argument, especially since he treats intellectual universals as the real sources of kinds, seen from a distance. On that view, they are substances just as an individual is an example of a nature. Here, “universal” means the nature’s indeterminacy; “intelligible” means the concept as it exists in thought. — س ره
